title: Eat this scroll (Ezekiel 3:1–3)
hookLine: the prophet eats a scroll and it is "as honey for sweetness"

cards: "Open thy mouth, and eat that I give thee." That's what Ezekiel hears, right after the vision. A hand reaches toward him, holding a scroll.
It's unrolled before him, and it's written on both sides, front and back. And the text tells us what's written there: lamentations, and mourning, and woe. A scroll of bad news, inside and out.
Not a scroll to read aloud, or file away, or hand to someone else. He is told to eat it.

teach.b: Here is how the text tells it, in the King James words: "Son of man, cause thy belly to eat, and fill thy bowels with this roll that I give thee. Then did I eat it; and it was in my mouth as honey for sweetness."
Stop on that. The words on the scroll are grief.
The taste is honey. The message hasn't changed; it's still lamentation and woe, and the rest of his book will be full of hard news. What changes is that it's no longer outside him.
He's swallowed it, and the word of God, even when it's heavy, tastes sweet in his mouth. Notice the order too.
Before he speaks a single word to the exiles, he takes the words in. Only then is he told: go, get thee unto the house of Israel, and speak with my words unto them.
The book of Psalms has a line close to this: the judgments of the Lord are sweeter than honey and the honeycomb. And Jewish life has a custom that makes the picture real.
In some communities, on a child's first day of learning Hebrew letters, honey is put on the letters, or on a slate, and the child licks it off. Learning should taste sweet.
The scroll Ezekiel eats isn't a children's lesson. It's hard. But the image holds both: words you take all the way in, even difficult ones, can become part of you, and that can be sweet.

how: Jews read Ezekiel 2–3 as the prophet's call, and some communities mark a child's first lesson in Hebrew letters with honey so that learning tastes sweet.

games.q: you're Ezekiel. a hand holds out a scroll of mourning and woe and tells you to eat it. what happens?
o: it tastes as honey for sweetness.
games.why: he eats it, and it is in his mouth as honey for sweetness, even though the words are grief.

practice: Pick one line you've read recently, from scripture, a book, a letter, or use Ezekiel's: it was in my mouth as honey for sweetness.

Say it slowly under your breath, then again, slower, letting each word sit the way you'd hold something sweet in your mouth, and notice which word has the most taste. If you pray, you can let that line become your prayer for now.
